servicesIndustries.name: Wholesale Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Wholesale trade is driven by business investment and trade flows. Sector GDP rose 0.9% month-over-month while remaining 1.9% below year-ago levels.1 The more current monthly wholesale series recorded a 1.9% sales gain in March 2026, beating a 1.4% consensus expectation, with Q1 2026 wholesale sales up 1.8% versus Q1 2025.2

The machinery, equipment and supplies subsector advanced 6.5% to $19.5B, with computer and communications equipment up 17.9% to $5.9B; personal and household goods rose 0.8% to $13.3B.2 The wholesale recovery tracks the manufacturing turnaround, with the manufacturing PMI at 53.3, alongside import flows.2 Wholesale carries no discrete project pipeline by design — distribution and warehousing capital is captured under NAICS 48-49 — so the sector is monitored through the StatCan wholesale series rather than database project linkage.3

servicesIndustries.name: Retail Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Retail trade is driven by consumer spending and confidence. Sector GDP rose 0.2% month-over-month and 2.3% year-over-year.1 Retail sales increased 0.7% to $72.1 billion in February 2026, a 3.8% year-over-year gain, and the advance estimate for March was +0.6% month-over-month, a third consecutive monthly increase.2

The March GDP detail showed retail trade decreased on the month, partly offsetting wholesale and transportation gains, indicating the monthly GDP and sales series diverged.1,2 The Bank of Canada outlook notes consumer discretionary spending remains pressured by trade tensions and slow household income growth.3 Retail carries no discrete project pipeline by design; retail capital is embedded in commercial_mixed projects tracked under NAICS 53, including the Oakridge Park 650,000 sq ft retail component opening spring 2026.3 If discretionary spending stays constrained, retail GDP momentum would moderate.

servicesIndustries.name: Transportation & Warehousing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Transportation and warehousing is driven by business activity and trade volumes. Sector GDP rose 1.2% month-over-month and 4.5% year-over-year, the strongest year-over-year reading among all 20 NAICS industries.1 Transport Canada is working with railways to cut freight rates for interprovincial steel and lumber beginning spring 2026, with rail terminal expansion and double-tracking underway nationally.2

The project database tracks 612 transport, rail and port projects totalling $44.13B, of which 155 are new in the last 21 days.3 These projects carry fuel-cost exposure as WTI sits at $100.16/bbl, up 62.5% year-over-year.3 The TSX infrastructure basket stood at 55.94, up 28.5% year-over-year, coinciding with Ontario's $210B 10-year transit-heavy capital plan.3 Canada's ports serve a $1.9 trillion international-trade economy, with containerized cargo projected at a 4.33% CAGR through 2031.2 If the spring 2026 rail-rate relief proceeds, interprovincial freight economics would shift.

servicesIndustries.name: Information & Cultural Industries
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Information and cultural industries are driven by technology investment and consumer spending. Sector GDP rose 0.7% month-over-month and 3.0% year-over-year.1 The federal sovereign large-scale AI data-centre program ran a call for proposals over 100 MW from January 15 to February 15 2026, and the Government of Canada and TELUS advanced a Vancouver and Kamloops data-centre cluster scaling from 85 MW to 150 MW by 2032 on 98% clean hydro; Bell named Bird Construction for its Sherwood AI data centre in Saskatchewan.2

The project database tracks 84 technology and telecom projects totalling $71.55B, of which 40 are new in the last 21 days.3 Canada's data-centre market is sized at USD 13.06B in 2026, up from USD 11.46B in 2025, projected to reach USD 25.09B by 2031 at a 13.95% CAGR.2 Telecom cumulative network investment reached $64.4B since 2020, while culture-sector nominal GDP was $16.7B in Q3 2025, up 0.2%.2 If sovereign AI proposals proceed, data-centre capital and coupled NAICS 22 electricity demand would expand.

servicesIndustries.name: Finance & Insurance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Finance and insurance is driven by interest rates and credit conditions. Sector GDP rose 0.3% month-over-month in February 2026 and 2.9% year-over-year.1 The Bank of Canada policy rate held at 2.25%, defining credit conditions across banking, insurance and payments.2 The sector generates $167 billion in GDP, equal to 8.5% of total economic output, with the six largest banks holding 93% of banking assets.3

The 2026 Spring Economic Update introduced measures on national investment, banking competition, housing support, and financial-crime reduction affecting banking, insurance and payments.3 Q1 2026 GDP is tracking near 1.7% on the TD estimate after a Q4 2025 contraction.3 Finance carries no discrete capital pipeline as a services industry; office-space demand overlaps the 277 NAICS-53 real estate projects.3 If open-banking and competition reform from the Spring Economic Update advances, sector structure would shift over the medium term.

servicesIndustries.name: Real Estate & Rental/Leasing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Real estate and rental/leasing is driven by mortgage rates, immigration and housing policy. Sector GDP was flat month-over-month and up 1.4% year-over-year.1 National housing starts rose 6% year-over-year in 2025 to 259,000 units, with the current seasonally adjusted annual rate at 279,317; CMHC projects starts to decline across 2026-2028 on elevated costs, softer demand and higher inventories, with the BoC policy rate at 2.25% shaping mortgage costs.2,3

The project database tracks 277 residential and commercial_mixed projects totalling $59.72B, of which 38 are new in the last 21 days.4 Toronto condo resale prices are down 15-18% from the 2022 peak, and rental starts exceeded condo apartment starts in the City of Toronto for the first time.4 Bill C-4, the First-Time Home Buyers' GST/HST Rebate of up to $50,000 on new homes, became law March 12 2026.4 If Bill C-4 relief and the condo-to-rental shift continue, purpose-built rental capital would hold while condo presale volume stays soft.

industrySources.title: Bank of Canada — Policy interest rate

servicesIndustries.name: Professional, Scientific & Technical Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Professional, scientific and technical services is driven by infrastructure project activity and business investment. Sector GDP declined 0.2% month-over-month and 0.9% year-over-year, in contrast with full-year 2024 growth of 2.2%, which outpaced the 2.0% overall economy.1,2

By province, 2024 sector GDP was $26.3B in British Columbia, equal to 7.99% of provincial output, $19.4B in Alberta at 5.06%, and $74.4B in Ontario at 8.6% of 2023 provincial GDP.2 The sector carries no discrete capital pipeline by design; engineering, architecture and IT services support the 1,075 NAICS-23 infrastructure projects and 84 NAICS-51 technology projects, including AI-data-centre and critical-minerals engineering demand.3 If AI-data-centre and critical-minerals engineering demand sustains, professional-services activity tied to NAICS 23 and 51 would stabilize.

servicesIndustries.name: Management of Companies & Enterprises
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Management of companies and enterprises is driven by the broader corporate-investment cycle. Sector GDP fell 2.6% month-over-month and 22.3% year-over-year, the steepest year-over-year contraction among all 20 NAICS industries; the figure is reported as published by Statistics Canada.1

No significant standalone developments occurred this week; activity is embedded in corporate-headquarters and holding-company structures rather than discrete projects, so the sector carries no project pipeline by design.2 The sector moves with the corporate-investment cycle, where oil-and-gas capex is rising from $50B to $57B and the manufacturing PMI stands at 53.3.2 The April Labour Force Survey recorded business, building and support services, the broader NAICS 55/56 grouping, adding 22,000 jobs, indicating output and the labour grouping are not moving together.3 If the corporate-investment cycle stabilizes alongside the manufacturing turnaround, the head-office output series would narrow its decline.

servicesIndustries.name: Administrative & Waste Management Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Administrative and waste management services is driven by business activity and regulatory programs. Sector GDP fell 0.8% month-over-month and 1.4% year-over-year, while the broader business, building and support services grouping added 22,000 jobs in the April 2026 Labour Force Survey, the largest sector gain, indicating the labour and GDP series diverged.1,2

The Environment Journal 2026 Top 25 Remediation Projects total $5.03 billion, covering nuclear-waste cleanup, mining remediation and brownfield redevelopment, with the Kitchener Green Residential Subdivision ($63M) ranked tenth.3 The project database tracks 18 environment and waste-management projects totalling $2.46B, of which 2 are new in the last 21 days; the discrete pipeline covers a subset of the broader slate.4 The Federal Contaminated Sites Action Plan continues under ECCC.3 In 2024 the sector had 110,597 non-employer and 53,288 employer establishments, with 52.1% micro-businesses.3 If the FCSAP and Top-25 slate deploy as scheduled, remediation-services activity would expand.

industrySources.title: Statistics Canada — Labour Force Survey April 2026

servicesIndustries.name: Educational Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Educational services is driven by government budgets and demographics. Sector GDP declined 0.5% month-over-month and 2.1% year-over-year, while the construction pipeline added 5 new projects in 21 days, indicating GDP output and the construction pipeline diverged.1,2

Ontario is investing $1 billion+ over five years from 2025-26 for postsecondary renewal, supporting campus real-estate intensification.3 The project database tracks 150 education projects totalling $5.26B.2 The University of Toronto unveiled the Temerty Building, a nine-storey, 388,000 sq ft facility consolidating the Faculty of Medicine and Arts & Science at King's College Circle on the St. George campus.3 The UBC Gateway Health Building ($189.91M) targets 2026 occupancy, and Camosun College's engineering renovation begins construction in fall 2026.3 If the Ontario renewal program and major campus projects proceed, education construction labour demand would continue.

servicesIndustries.name: Health Care & Social Assistance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Health care and social assistance is driven by demographics and government budgets. Sector GDP was flat month-over-month and up 2.1% year-over-year, with health care and social assistance adding 18,000 jobs in the April 2026 Labour Force Survey.1,2

British Columbia is delivering more than $6.4 billion in new hospital construction starting 2025-2026, covering 30 hospital and health-facility projects, 11 long-term-care centres and four cancer centres across five health regions; Quebec allocated $2.3 billion over 10 years for hospital construction in its 2026-27 budget.3 The project database tracks 253 healthcare projects totalling $21.07B, of which 19 are new in the last 21 days.4 Flagship builds include the New St. Paul's Hospital in Vancouver (1.2M sq ft, complete 2026, open 2027) and the Dawson Creek hospital ($590M, approximately 92% complete).3 If BC's and Quebec's programs deploy as budgeted, long-term-care and cancer-centre capital would expand.

industrySources.title: Statistics Canada — Labour Force Survey April 2026

servicesIndustries.name: Arts, Entertainment & Recreation
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Arts, entertainment and recreation is driven by consumer spending and tourism. Sector GDP fell 2.5% month-over-month while remaining up 0.2% year-over-year.1 BC Place in Vancouver was upgraded to host seven FIFA World Cup 2026 matches, expected to attract more than 350,000 fans and generate roughly $1 billion in additional BC visitor spending across 2026-31.2

The International Convention Attraction Fund secured 116 events, drawing approximately 324,200 attendees with $803.3M in direct impact as of March 2026, and federal funding allocated $726,000 to the Corleck Building cultural space in Toronto.2 The project database tracks approximately 143 tourism_culture projects totalling $22B, shared with NAICS 72.3 Ontario NAICS 71 employed 177,700 in 2024 with more than $8.2B in GDP, while Quebec job growth across 2024-2026 is expected negative on changed consumer habits and funding lag.2 If FIFA World Cup 2026 demand materializes as projected, venue and event activity would rise.

industrySources.title: ISED — International event funding and tourism

servicesIndustries.name: Accommodation & Food Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Accommodation and food services is driven by tourism, business travel and consumer spending. Sector GDP declined 0.2% month-over-month while rising 3.1% year-over-year, with accommodation and food services adding 13,000 jobs in the April 2026 Labour Force Survey.1,2

The Canada hotel construction pipeline reached record Q1 2026 levels with 331 hotel projects covering 45,401 rooms; Ontario leads with 190 projects and 27,567 rooms, equal to 57% of the pipeline, and Toronto holds 71 projects with 11,420 rooms.3 The project database tracks approximately 143 tourism_culture projects totalling $22B, shared with NAICS 71.4 Canada's hospitality market is sized at USD 21.34B in 2026, projected to reach USD 27.46B by 2031 at a 5.18% CAGR, with about 1.9M workers, roughly 9.5% of national employment.3 If the 45,401-room pipeline proceeds while reduced international-student and temporary-work permits constrain labour supply, operating capacity would lag construction.

servicesIndustries.name: Other Services (except Public Administration)
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Other services is driven by consumer discretionary spending and demographics. Sector GDP rose 0.3% month-over-month and 0.6% year-over-year, a near-flat movement tracked through StatCan GDP-by-industry.1 No significant standalone capital developments occurred this week; personal, repair, civic and religious organizations are research-led with no discrete project pipeline by design.2

The sector moves with consumer discretionary spending, which the Bank of Canada outlook notes is pressured by trade tensions and slow household-income growth, with the BoC policy rate held at 2.25% shaping consumer credit conditions.2,3 The repair and maintenance, personal and laundry services, and religious, grant-making and civic organization subsectors track household spending patterns rather than capital formation, so the sector is monitored via the StatCan output series rather than database project linkage.2 If trade tensions continue pressuring household income, Other-Services demand would stay near-flat.

industrySources.title: Bank of Canada — Monetary Policy Report

servicesIndustries.name: Public Administration
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration is driven by government budgets and policy priorities. Sector GDP declined 0.5% month-over-month while rising 0.3% year-over-year.1 The federal 2026-27 Main Estimates present $502.8 billion in budgetary spending, comprising $230.4B voted and $272.4B statutory, with Department of Finance planned spending of $158.3B.2

The project database tracks 207 government, defence and Indigenous projects totalling $82.48B, of which 11 are new in the last 21 days.3 Canada achieved the NATO 2% GDP defence-spending target in 2025-26, and Phase 2 military housing covers approximately 7,500 residential housing units across 25 sites at more than $3.7B, with CFB Gagetown infrastructure completed in March 2026.4 Defence Investment Agency legislation in Spring 2026 moves Defence Construction Canada under the DIA.4 If the DIA legislation passes and Phase 2 military housing proceeds, public-administration-linked construction would expand.
